coverage: Nine stories · AI safety, chips, teens, health, quantum computing and space

cards.headline: OpenAI says it will report when AI goes off track
cards.summary: OpenAI says it will regularly publish reports about unexpected or unauthorized behavior by its AI systems. Its new framework describes how employees can flag cases for investigation and how the company will decide what to disclose.
cards.whyItMatters: Powerful software can behave differently from what its creators intended. Testing, monitoring and transparent reporting are part of figuring out whether AI systems are working safely.

csp.connection: Computing systems need testing and oversight because their behavior can affect users and other systems.

cards.headline: Huawei says demand is outrunning its AI chip supply
cards.summary: Huawei says it cannot make enough AI computing equipment to meet demand in China and is limiting overseas sales. The company is also preparing new AI chips as it competes with Nvidia in specialized hardware for running large AI systems.
cards.whyItMatters: AI is not only a software story. The number, speed and availability of physical processors can determine who can build and run powerful models.

csp.connection: Software capabilities depend on the hardware resources available to execute computations.

cards.headline: A $1 billion award backs a quantum-chip factory
cards.summary: IBM-owned Anderon finalized a $1 billion U.S. government award for research and development at its 300-millimeter quantum-wafer foundry in New York. IBM says the facility is designed to manufacture quantum wafers for customers across the developing quantum industry.
cards.whyItMatters: Quantum computing still faces major engineering challenges. Building shared manufacturing infrastructure is one step toward turning laboratory prototypes into technology that more researchers can actually use.

csp.connection: New kinds of computing require both algorithms and specialized physical hardware to run them.

cards.headline: A new study asks teens what they think about AI
cards.summary: Google published findings from research with RXN about how teenagers view and use AI. The study focuses on teens' curiosity, concerns and expectations, giving designers another source of evidence about the people actually using these tools.
cards.whyItMatters: Students are not just passive users of technology. Research about teen experiences can influence how AI products are designed, taught and evaluated.

csp.connection: The effects of computing innovations can differ among groups, so designers need information from the people affected.

cards.headline: Europe proposes new social-media limits for young people
cards.summary: The European Union's top official proposed banning social-media accounts for children under 13 and placing limits on accounts for older teens. The proposal still has to be debated and approved by EU member countries, so it is not yet law.
cards.whyItMatters: Rules about age, algorithms and account design could change how platforms work for young users. It also shows how software design choices can become public-policy questions.

csp.connection: Computing platforms can create social effects that lead governments and communities to debate rules for their design and use.

cards.headline: AI matches live X-rays with 3D scans in seconds
cards.summary: MIT researchers developed a patient-specific system called xvr that matches X-rays taken during surgery with earlier 3D CT or MRI scans. In research tests, the model aligned the images within seconds and with sub-millimeter precision; it is a research technique, not an established treatment.
cards.whyItMatters: This is AI doing a very different job from writing text or making pictures. It shows how algorithms can combine medical images to help humans navigate complex physical spaces.

csp.connection: Computers can transform and compare different representations of data to extract useful information.

cards.headline: A routine data check found a brand-new Moon crater
cards.summary: A scientist checking Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images noticed an unusual bright spot and compared older and newer Moon maps. NASA says the comparison revealed the largest newly formed crater yet found in the solar system.
cards.whyItMatters: Big discoveries can begin with careful data inspection. Computers make it possible to store, map and compare years of images so scientists can spot changes that would otherwise be easy to miss.

csp.connection: Large image datasets can be compared across time to identify patterns and changes.

cards.headline: Earth's center moves as water shifts around the planet
cards.summary: NASA scientists track tiny seasonal shifts in Earth's center of mass as water moves among oceans, land and ice. That moving reference point matters for satellite navigation and precise measurements of elevation.
cards.whyItMatters: GPS-like systems depend on mathematical reference points that are more complicated than they look. Even fractions of an inch can matter when scientists combine satellite data from around the world.

csp.connection: Precise computing systems depend on consistent reference data and measurements that can be updated as conditions change.

cards.headline: The computer-graphics teapot is still teaching after 50 years
cards.summary: University of Utah researchers are looking back at the Utah Teapot, a simple 3D model created in 1975 that became a standard test object in computer graphics. The model has been used across research, software, movies, games and digital art.
cards.whyItMatters: A useful test dataset does not have to be huge. A shared 3D object helped generations of programmers compare rendering ideas and improve the graphics behind modern games and films.

csp.connection: Digital models are data representations that programs can transform into images using algorithms.
